title: Exploding Kittens & The Key to Running a Successful Kickstarter | Elan Lee | Talks at Google
description:
Elan Lee recently visited Google to talk about the work that went into the record-setting Exploding Kittens Kickstarter. He discusses how his groundbreaking work on Alternate Reality games such as The Beast and Ilovebees made him aware of the power of positive, online communities and he describes how his analysis of previous Kickstarter campaigns showed him the connection between daily community engagement and acquiring new backers.

You can check out his latest Kickstarter for Throw Throw Burrito, a dodgeball/card game at https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/elanlee/throw-throw-burrito.
summary: The speaker recounts his transition from building digital products to creating a physical card game after realizing his work contributed to social isolation. He explains that the game, originally named Bomb Squad, was renamed Exploding Kittens based on a suggestion from his friend Matthew Inman to make the concept less obvious and more adorable.

She was the lead actor on almost all the phone calls, and she was one of the main characters in the game. We gave her the number of the payphone that we were pretty sure he was going to call, and we had her manually call it. And it just rang and rang and rang. And she called me and she said, he didn't answer. Call again. Ring and ring. He didn't answer. Call again. And after like 40 minutes of calling, he actually answered the phone in the middle of this crazy hurricane, and I wish I had the audio recording of the insanity this poor guy went through. But she had to break character and say, go home. This is-- you are above and beyond. You're great. You're amazing. Go home. This is not worth it. And we had-- what was really funny is the night before we launched this campaign. So I have to check everything with Microsoft before launching something insane like this. And I really like to give them no warning at all or ability to change things. So I submitted the entire design doc to them the night before launch and said, this is what we're going-- this is how we've already spent all your money. This is what we're going to launch tomorrow. 9:00 AM is when we're going. And their lawyer read it and called me up that night at 10:00 PM and he said, I love this. This is the most creative thing I've ever seen. This is going to be so good. I love it. We just need you to make one small change. You can't use payphones. And it was like, OK, yeah, got it. Sure. We'll cancel payphones. Got it. And hung up and of course just launched it anyway. But it turns out he was right. Payphones were really dumb idea, and it almost got some poor kid killed. AUDIENCE: Hi. Have you tried any AR games? ELAN LEE: Quite a bit. Yeah. I really like AR. I have not yet seen an AR game that I think is not isolating, not very lonely-making, but I play them all, I have all of the systems, and I'm still waiting for that thing to reach out and capture my attention. AUDIENCE: Hi. Thanks so much for coming today. It was a really great talk. I did miss the first five minutes, so if you already covered this, feel free to just tell me to go watch the video on YouTube later. Cards Against Humanity came out about four years before Exploding Kittens. ELAN LEE: About eight years. Yeah. AUDIENCE: Oh, eight years. OK. I just googled that, so something is wrong with Google. Can somebody check into that? OK. So did that have a big influence on changing the mentality of how we're playing games? Because I grew up playing games. Like you were talking about, sometimes, they're very isolating. Sometimes they're family games and group games with your siblings. And for me, Cards Against humanity was kind of a breakthrough into, oh, yeah, I like gaming. I forgot that I like to play games. And I don't want to be isolated and wearing some AR/VR kind of outfit to do it. ELAN LEE: Yeah, it's a great point. Maybe I've got the year wrong if you've googled it. AUDIENCE: Google is never wrong. ELAN LEE: Yeah. Cards Against Humanity started as a Kickstarter project. So whenever they came out, it's actually very well-documented. They changed everything. Like you said, they kind of reminded people that games were fun. But the way they did it-- I'm very good friends with them. I love that game. I've played probably more of that game than anyone else on the planet. And it's because-- what I learned from that game, and what I think kind of every all game designers learned from that is that games should not be entertaining. Games should make the people you're playing with entertaining. And previously, before Cards Against Humanity-- like, when you look at games from the '50s through the '80s, games worked so hard to be entertaining. Monopoly, and UNO, and the Game of Life, and Stratego, and all of these games-- which I play all the time and I really like-- they were trying very hard to be as entertaining as possible. Cards Against Humanity said, no, screw that. The whole concept is the people you're playing with have to be the entertainment value. And when I sat down to design Exploding Kittens, that was like written on my wall. And if you look at the game with kind of a keen design eye, every card in Exploding Kittens is designed to create a relationship between you and another player at the table-- very, very specifically designed that way-- because the mantra is, create a relationship. Let them have fun on their own. Create another relationship. Let them have fun on their own. And that relationship can be positive, or adversarial, or whatever it is. But it has to be them. You have to cede the control over to them. And I think that's what Cards Against Humanity kind of taught the gaming world and ushered in this incredible renaissance of tabletop gaming. AUDIENCE: And I think that you probably drew a lot of influence from UNO, I would guess, in Exploding Kittens. ELAN LEE: Yeah. Our game gets compared to UNO quite a bit. UNO is like the game I was raised on. And so whatever I do is based on UNO, whether I like it or not. AUDIENCE: Yeah, you got to skip a turn. AUDIENCE: So I went to ask as far as electronic games or video games that could be said to not be isolating, are you aware of, for example, the Jackbox Party games? ELAN LEE: Yeah. Jackbox Party games are a great example of non-isolating games. The other one that I've spent way too much time playing is Spaceteam. If anyone's played that on your iPhone or Android phone, that game for me is like the epitome of, make the people you're playing with the entertainment. If you don't have it, go download this game. It is really just the finest thing out there. All of the Jackbox series-- I think they've got like seven series out there now-- like seven different versions-- it's probably like 80% of them are just spectacular. And so you buy a pack, and there's like seven or eight games in there, and you will love, love five of them. And that's a pretty good ratio for a giant pack of games. So, yeah. There's a lot of stuff like that. But really, the litmus test for me is just like, what is the point of this game? Is this game trying to entertain me, or is it trying to make the people I'm playing with entertaining? And games that so clearly pass that are the games I love and cherish and spend all my time playing with my friends. AUDIENCE: Can you also share some-- related question-- can you also share some insight on like that game that you play with your friends physically with you versus-- ELAN LEE: I will just say, just because I love plugging this game, and there's a game out there called Happy Salmon. It's a physical card game. It is the game I have played most in the last year and a half probably. I think it's probably the finest game on the market. Go buy this game. It's an $8 or $10 investment. Go buy. This game the game lasts 90 seconds start to finish, and I've never played it for less than two hours, because the moment you're done, you just want to play again. It is a game-- I'm tempted to just tell you how to play. But you really should see the cards. It'll take you five minutes to learn. But this game involves a lot of very, very fast and casual physical contact-- high-fiving people, fist-bumping people, running in a circle around people-- and the endorphins and the adrenaline that result from this super, super simple game. If you are not smiling and laughing while playing this game, you have no soul. And it is games like that that allow people to celebrate their group of friends, their playmates, that I think are currently, we're watching, they're changing the world right now. The board game industry went from a few tens of millions of dollars a year to now well over a billion, and that's because of games-- it's because of this renaissance. It's because people are getting a little bit overwhelmed by their screens. Obviously, screens will always be a part of our lives, but people are starting to say, look, there has to be time when we walk away from these things. There has to be a few moments at night, a few moments on the weekends, whatever it is, where we just enjoy the people we're around, and to have the tools to enable us to do so are becoming more and more a welcome addition into all of our homes AUDIENCE: Yeah, but to add that, the bandwidth is increasing. When these guys are playing games, actually, they talk to their friends. Like, even though they're not physically with them, and maybe there could be some like video, or virtual reality, or whatever to connect them. ELAN LEE: Not only do I agree with that, but we're definitely starting to see it, right? Like, as the bandwidth goes up, as the communities are being more and more emphasized in the world of video games, those kinds of interactions are certainly increasing. And it's really exciting to see, and it's so necessary. So I'm very excited about it. I used to be 100% anti-screen. But we now did an Exploding Kittens mobile game, specifically because we realized, look, we don't-- there's ways to do this. There's ways to encourage people that, although they're looking at a screen, to still celebrate the people they're playing with, the people in the room, to laugh out loud, pass your phone around. And so all those things are very, very doable, and some of the smartest people out there are working on it. And I love that we're all sort of stealing and collaborating and helping each other accomplish that goal. So it's such an exciting time to be building games right now. AUDIENCE: So, so much of what you've done has been building communities to build your products. But what do you do when communities become too big and then negative influences start to kind of percolate. ELAN LEE: Yeah. So here's a great example that. The very first alternate reality game I worked on was called The Beast, and it was a project associated with Steven Spielberg's movie "AI." Spielberg asked me to essentially build a sequel to the movie "AI" and then we would release it before "AI" and let people live in that world before the movie came out. And me and my team spent six months building this thing, and we spent six months building six months worth of content, and the idea was, look, the audience is going to take six months to go through this content. And while they're going through all the content we've built, we'll spend that time building another six months of content. So we'll have a year-long game built over the course of a staggered year. And we should be fine. And the first day, so many people showed up that they digested all six months worth of content in 20 minutes. That was a very big crowd. And it got really scary. At that moment, we realized this is a different kind of game. And we have to play it and create it in real time. And I'd say when giant audiences show up, there's two very important things you have to do. One is you have to stop thinking about this as a pre-canned thing. It must be collaborative. It must be created and edited and adjusted in real time, so that it feels alive, so that that many brains throwing themselves at this thing feel like they're throwing it at a living entity that is worth their time and attention. And the second thing is you have to delegate to the actual community. And there is no way we can read every message posted, every tweet, every Facebook post. There's no way. There's just too much. And so you have to start reaching out to the community, assigning managers, assigning moderators, and entrusting them to filter up the most relevant things, so that you immediately do know when things are broken, when things need adjustment. And you'll often get it wrong, and you have to adjust your community management as well. But it's so important to share the reigns with the community. Otherwise, you have no chance of success. AUDIENCE: So you talked about how the initial idea was seeing kids play. So a lot of the photos in the Kickstarter campaign were adults playing. Can you talk a little more about designing games for kids and adults to play together, or like what you learned about, that sort of thing? ELAN LEE: Yeah. That's a great point. So the reason that most of the pictures are adults is all of those pictures are from the Kickstarter campaign. And to just open a Kickstarter account, you have to be 18 or older. So that was a very easy filter for those first 30 days. Now our largest demographic is ages seven to 12. And what happens there is kind of by accident. I think if we had set out to build a game for seven- to 12-year-olds, we would have failed. It's because we built a game for us, who have sort of the mental capacity of like a 16-year-old, because we aimed for like maybe 16 to 18, it hit 16 to 18, and 16 to 30, or 16 to 40 really well. But it also appealed to that younger crowd who felt like, I can participate in this thing. I'm older. I am more sophisticated. I'm a little bit-- I'm a little bit better able to handle this than my parents thought I was. And the game does not dumb itself down for them. It tells adult jokes-- not inappropriate jokes. We have a whole separate game for that called Exploding Kittens: Not Safe for Work. But the core game is built with slightly crude humor that I don't think any parent would object to, but the kids-- specifically literally seven-year-olds-- look at this and think, oh, man. I'm the big kid now. I get to play this thing, and laugh at it, and laugh with my parents, because they're laughing at the exact same jokes that I'm laughing at. And we kind of did that by accident. It just happens to be where Matt's sense of humor, where my sensibility is, and we stumbled into it by accident. One of the beautiful side effects of that, which I did not see coming at all, is about once or twice a month, we get a letter from a family psychiatrist, because apparently this game has worked its way into that community and is used as a tool. And we get these letters saying, thank you so much for creating this game. We use it for family therapy sessions, where young children like 10 and under have lost the ability to communicate with their parents, and vice versa. And we use your game-- we make them play together-- as a way to force that communication, because every card played, like I said, was designed to create those interactions. Another way to phrase that-- every card played forces a conversation of some sort. And it's certainly not something we designed for, but it is so amazing and so rewarding to see this thing actually helping young kids communicate with their families, where otherwise all those lines of communication had broken down. SPEAKER 1: Thank you once again for joining us and please give him a round of applause. [APPLAUSE] ELAN LEE: Thanks, everyone.
